objective: Informational texts provide information related to a particular idea, distinct from fiction.；Text features include text organizers (index, table of contents, glossary), graphic aids (maps, charts, diagrams), and typographic effects (bold, italics, font size).；Background knowledge significantly impacts comprehension of informational texts.

learningGoals.statement: Identify and describe the function of text features (organizers, graphic aids, typographic effects) in informational texts.
Adjust reading strategies based on text type (fiction vs. informational).
Apply background knowledge to enhance comprehension of informational texts.
Evaluate the effectiveness of vocabulary learning strategies, distinguishing between memorization and active use.
Critique over-reliance on translation tools for reading informational texts.

knowledgeNodes.name: 信息文本
knowledgeNodes.definition: Texts that provide information related to a particular idea, often using text features like organizers, graphic aids, and typographic effects.

knowledgeNodes.name: 文本特征
knowledgeNodes.definition: Structural elements in informational texts that help readers locate and understand information, including text organizers, graphic aids, and typographic effects.

knowledgeNodes.name: 文本组织者
knowledgeNodes.definition: Macro-level architecture of a document such as indexes, prefaces, tables of contents, glossaries, and appendices that help manage data location.

knowledgeNodes.name: 图形辅助
knowledgeNodes.definition: Visual elements like maps, charts, diagrams, photographs that compress complex information into readable formats.

knowledgeNodes.name: 排版效果
knowledgeNodes.definition: Manipulation of font size, style, or color to guide reader's eye to critical vocabulary and create visual hierarchy.

knowledgeNodes.name: 阅读策略
knowledgeNodes.definition: Approaches for reading informational texts, including using background knowledge and asking strategic questions about author's perspective and evidence.

knowledgeNodes.name: 反馈公式
knowledgeNodes.definition: Structure for giving feedback: something liked + something that didn't work + something to do differently next time.

knowledgeNodes.name: 退出票
knowledgeNodes.definition: End-of-lesson reflection answering three things learned, two things unsure, one question.

questions.stem: When you see a table of contents and headings in a textbook, what is their main purpose?
questions.successCriteria: Recognizes that text features help locate and organize information.
questions.ossdExpectation: Reading for Meaning: read and demonstrate an understanding of a variety of informational texts.
questions.stemIntent: Check if student sees text features as functional rather than decorative.
questions.commonMisconception: Belief that features like headings and charts are only for decoration.

options.label: A
options.text: To make the page look more interesting and break up the text.
options.feedbackWrong: Text features are not just decorative; they help readers navigate and understand the structure of the text.

options.label: B
options.text: To quickly locate sections and understand the organization of the content.
options.feedbackCorrect: Correct! Table of contents and headings are functional tools that help readers find and organize information.

options.label: C
options.text: To add decoration between paragraphs.
options.feedbackWrong: That is not their main purpose. They serve a navigational function.

options.label: D
options.text: To replace the need to read the full text.
options.feedbackWrong: They support reading, not replace it. You still need to read the text carefully.

questions.stem: A student always uses Google Translate for every unfamiliar word when reading an English informational text. Which statement best critiques this strategy?
questions.successCriteria: Recognizes that over-reliance on translation hinders development of reading strategies like inferring meaning in context.
questions.ossdExpectation: Reading for Meaning: read and demonstrate an understanding of a variety of informational texts.
questions.stemIntent: Check if student understands the downside of heavy translation tool use.
questions.commonMisconception: Belief that translation tools are always beneficial with no drawbacks for learning.

options.label: A
options.text: It is efficient and helps you understand everything immediately.
options.feedbackWrong: While it may give quick answers, it prevents you from developing the ability to infer meaning from context.

options.label: B
options.text: It prevents you from practicing skills like inferring meaning from context and building inference skills.
options.feedbackCorrect: Correct! Relying on translation circumvents the active process of figuring out meaning, which is essential for language growth.

options.label: C
options.text: It is the best way to learn new vocabulary because you see the translation immediately.
options.feedbackWrong: Seeing a translation does not necessarily lead to long-term retention or correct usage. Active engagement is more effective.

options.label: D
options.text: It is only bad if the translation is inaccurate; otherwise it is fine.
options.feedbackWrong: Even accurate translations can create dependency and reduce opportunities for deep processing of the language.

questions.stem: A student memorizes a list of 20 new vocabulary words every week but never uses them in speaking or writing. What is the most likely outcome?
questions.successCriteria: Understands that memorization without use leads to poor retention and application.
questions.ossdExpectation: Reading for Meaning: read and demonstrate an understanding of a variety of informational texts.
questions.stemIntent: Check if student understands the ineffectiveness of rote memorization without active use.
questions.commonMisconception: Belief that memorizing definitions is sufficient for vocabulary learning.

options.label: A
options.text: They will quickly forget most of the words because they are not used in context.
options.feedbackCorrect: Correct! Without active use, words fade from memory. Practice in reading and writing reinforces learning.

options.label: B
options.text: They will have a large, permanent vocabulary that they can use correctly.
options.feedbackWrong: Memorization alone does not guarantee retention or correct usage. Context and use are essential.

options.label: C
options.text: Memorization is enough; they will be able to use the words correctly later.
options.feedbackWrong: Knowing a definition does not automatically translate to correct usage in sentences. Active practice is needed.

options.label: D
options.text: They should only memorize words they see often; that would be more efficient.
options.feedbackWrong: Frequency of exposure helps, but without use, even frequent words may not be retained or used well.

questions.stem: When reading a short story, you focus on plot and character emotions. When reading a science article, your reading approach should be:
questions.successCriteria: Recognizes that different text types require different reading strategies.
questions.ossdExpectation: Reading for Meaning: read and demonstrate an understanding of a variety of informational texts.
questions.stemIntent: Check if student understands that reading strategies need to be adjusted based on text type.
questions.commonMisconception: Treating all texts the same way, ignoring text features and purposes.

options.label: A
options.text: The same, because all reading requires the same skills.
options.feedbackWrong: Different genres demand different approaches. Informational texts require you to extract information, evaluate evidence, and use text features.

options.label: B
options.text: Focus on extracting information, evaluating evidence, and using text features like headings and diagrams.
options.feedbackCorrect: Correct! Science articles are informational texts; you need to read for main ideas, details, and to evaluate the author's claims.

options.label: C
options.text: Ignore text features and just read the paragraphs from start to finish.
options.feedbackWrong: Text features are designed to help you navigate and understand informational texts. Ignoring them makes reading less efficient.

options.label: D
options.text: Read faster to finish quickly, since it is just facts.
options.feedbackWrong: Speed reading may cause you to miss important details and nuances. Informational texts require careful reading.

questions.stem: Before reading a passage about climate change, you recall what you already know about weather patterns. How does this help your reading?
questions.successCriteria: Recognizes that prior knowledge facilitates comprehension and engagement with new information.
questions.ossdExpectation: Reading for Meaning: read and demonstrate an understanding of a variety of informational texts.
questions.stemIntent: Check if student values background knowledge as a reading strategy.
questions.commonMisconception: Underestimating or ignoring the role of background knowledge in comprehension.

options.label: A
options.text: It activates relevant schemas, making it easier to connect new information and understand the text better.
options.feedbackCorrect: Correct! Prior knowledge provides a framework for understanding and evaluating new information.

options.label: B
options.text: It is a waste of time because the text will provide all you need.
options.feedbackWrong: Texts do not always provide all necessary background. Activating prior knowledge enhances comprehension.

options.label: C
options.text: It only helps if you are an expert on the topic.
options.feedbackWrong: Even partial prior knowledge can be helpful. It gives you a starting point for understanding.

options.label: D
options.text: It might lead to bias, so you should avoid using it.
options.feedbackWrong: Being aware of potential bias is good, but using prior knowledge is generally beneficial. You can also evaluate how the text confirms or challenges your ideas.

questions.stem: In an informational text, a map of the New Forest National Park is included. The best reason for this graphic aid is to:
questions.successCriteria: Recognizes that graphic aids serve a functional purpose like providing spatial information.
questions.ossdExpectation: Reading for Meaning: read and demonstrate an understanding of a variety of informational texts.
questions.stemIntent: Check if student understands that graphic aids are not decorative but convey specific information.
questions.commonMisconception: Belief that charts and maps are only for decoration.

options.label: A
options.text: To fill empty space on the page and make it look more professional.
options.feedbackWrong: Maps serve a purpose: they provide visual information that supports the text.

options.label: B
options.text: Provide a visual representation of the area to help readers understand locations and spatial relationships.
options.feedbackCorrect: Correct! Maps, charts, and diagrams are functional tools that compress complex spatial data into an easily understood format.

options.label: C
options.text: To decorate the text and make it more colorful.
options.feedbackWrong: While they may be visually appealing, their primary function is informational, not decorative.

options.label: D
options.text: To replace the need to read the description of the park.
options.feedbackWrong: Graphic aids complement the text; they do not replace reading. Both work together to convey information.

questions.stem: When you look at the index of a textbook before reading, you are using a text organizer. This strategy is most helpful for:
questions.successCriteria: Recognizes that text organizers like index are more common and useful in informational texts than fiction.
questions.ossdExpectation: Reading for Meaning: read and demonstrate an understanding of a variety of informational texts.
questions.stemIntent: Check if student understands that text organizers are tailored for informational text navigation.
questions.commonMisconception: Treating informational texts like fiction without using their structural tools.

options.label: A
options.text: Fiction novels, because they also have indexes.
options.feedbackWrong: Indexes are rare in fiction; they are a feature of informational texts designed to help locate specific topics.

options.label: B
options.text: Informational texts, because they often contain indexes to help you find specific topics quickly.
options.feedbackCorrect: Correct! Indexes are typical in textbooks and reference books, allowing you to scan for specific information before deep reading.

options.label: C
options.text: Poetry, because poems often have a glossary.
options.feedbackWrong: Poetry may have glossaries, but indexes are more associated with non-fiction. The question specifically asks about index.

options.label: D
options.text: Any text equally; all texts have indexes.
options.feedbackWrong: Not all texts have indexes. They are most common in longer informational texts.

questions.stem: Explain why memorizing vocabulary without using it in reading or writing is an ineffective strategy for learning English. Provide one specific suggestion for improvement.
questions.successCriteria: Provides a clear reason and a concrete suggestion for active use.
questions.ossdExpectation: Reading for Meaning: read and demonstrate an understanding of a variety of informational texts.
questions.stemIntent: Check if student can critically evaluate a vocabulary learning strategy and propose improvement.
questions.commonMisconception: Belief that memorization alone suffices for vocabulary acquisition.
questions.rubric: Full marks (2 points): Clearly states that memorization without use leads to poor retention and inability to apply words correctly; provides a specific suggestion (e.g., write sentences, read articles, use words in speaking). Partial (1 point): Mentions the problem but suggestion is vague. No credit: Does not explain why it's ineffective or gives no suggestion.
questions.sampleStrongAnswer: Memorizing words without using them in context is ineffective because the brain does not form strong connections, leading to quick forgetting. To improve, I would try to write two original sentences with each new word and use them in class discussions to reinforce meaning and usage.

reteachModules.trigger: Student believes text features are only decorative and not functional.
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: Students think that text features like headings, charts, and indices are primarily for decoration and do not serve a functional role in comprehension.

miniLesson.explain: Text features in informational texts are functional tools that help readers navigate, locate, and understand information. They include text organizers (table of contents, index, glossary), graphic aids (maps, charts, diagrams), and typographic effects (bold, italics, font size). Ignoring them makes reading harder.
miniLesson.example: In your Grade 9 geography textbook, the table of contents helps you find the chapter on Canada. A diagram of a river shows how it erodes landforms. These are not decorations.
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Think: 'Features guide, not decorate.' Text features are like road signs – they direct you to information.

guidedPractice.prompt: What is the main purpose of a table of contents in a textbook?
guidedPractice.answer: To help locate sections and understand the organization of the content.

guidedPractice.prompt: You are reading an article about fire safety. It includes a diagram of a smoke detector. Explain why the diagram is helpful, not decorative.
guidedPractice.answer: The diagram shows how the smoke detector works visually, making it easier to understand than just text. It provides practical information.

guidedPractice.prompt: A classmate says, 'Headings and charts are just to make the text look nice. I always skip them.' Do you agree? Why or why not? Suggest a better approach.
guidedPractice.answer: I disagree. Headings and charts are functional. Headings organize content and help you predict what's next. Charts summarize data quickly. Skipping them wastes an opportunity to understand faster. Better approach: scan headings first, then read details, and use charts to see patterns.

reteachModules.trigger: Student selected incorrect option on question diag-olc4o-q2, indicating belief that translation tools are always beneficial.
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: Belief that translation tools always help learning with no drawbacks, ignoring the importance of developing inference skills.

miniLesson.explain: Using translation tools for every unknown word prevents you from practicing the skill of inferring meaning from context. This skill is critical for reading informational texts where you often encounter new vocabulary. Over-reliance on translation also reduces your ability to think in English and can slow down your reading speed. Instead, try to guess the meaning from surrounding words and sentences before reaching for a dictionary. Remember the feedback formula: like, didn't work, different. In this case: I liked that I understand the word; it didn't work because I didn't practice inference; next time I will try to guess first.
miniLesson.example: When reading a science article about climate change, you see the word 'precipitation'. Instead of immediately translating, look at context clues: 'The amount of precipitation, such as rain and snow, has increased.' From 'rain and snow', you can infer precipitation means water falling from the sky. This builds your ability to understand English naturally.
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Don't use a crutch; use context. Guess first, then check.

guidedPractice.prompt: True or False: Using Google Translate for every word you don't know is the best way to learn English vocabulary.
guidedPractice.answer: False. It prevents you from practicing inference skills and can create dependency.

guidedPractice.prompt: Your classmate says, 'I always use translation because it's faster and I understand everything.' List two reasons why this strategy might limit their English growth.
guidedPractice.answer: 1. It stops them from practicing guessing meaning from context, which is an important reading strategy. 2. It may lead to forgetting the word quickly because they didn't engage deeply with the word in context.

guidedPractice.prompt: Read this sentence from an informational text: 'The ecosystem was resilient, able to recover quickly from disturbances.' You are unsure what 'resilient' means. Describe the steps you would take to figure out its meaning WITHOUT using a translation tool, and explain how this process helps your learning.
guidedPractice.answer: Steps: 1. Look at context clues: 'able to recover quickly from disturbances' explains resilient. 2. Use background knowledge: ecosystems that bounce back are resilient. 3. Make a guess: probably 'able to recover easily'. 4. After reading, check with a dictionary to confirm. This process helps because it forces me to think in English, connect ideas, and remember the word better through active engagement.

reteachModules.trigger: Incorrect response on a diagnostic question targeting vocabulary memorization vs. active use (e.g., Q3 or Q8).
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: Many students believe that memorizing definitions alone is sufficient for vocabulary learning. They underestimate the importance of using new words in context (reading, writing, speaking) to retain and apply them.

miniLesson.explain: Memorizing vocabulary without using it in context is ineffective because the brain does not form strong connections. Words that are not used are quickly forgotten. To truly learn a word, you need to encounter it multiple times in meaningful contexts and practice using it actively. Learning a word is like learning a new skill: you have to practice it.
miniLesson.example: For example, a student memorizes a list of 8 new words from a science article but never uses them in sentences. A week later, they recall very few. Instead, if they write a short paragraph using 5-6 of the new words, they are more likely to remember them and use them correctly.
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Remember: 'Use it or lose it.' Just like exercising a muscle, vocabulary must be actively used to stay strong.

guidedPractice.prompt: True or False: Memorizing a list of vocabulary words without using them in sentences is an effective way to learn English. Explain why.
guidedPractice.answer: False. Without use, words are easily forgotten because the brain lacks strong connections to context and meaning.

guidedPractice.prompt: You just learned the word 'picturesque' from a text about the New Forest National Park. Write one sentence using 'picturesque' and explain how it helps you remember the word.
guidedPractice.answer: Example sentence: 'The New Forest National Park is a picturesque landscape with ancient woodlands.' Using the word in a sentence about the text helps me connect the word to a concrete image and context, making it easier to recall.

guidedPractice.prompt: A friend says, 'I don't need to use new words; I can just look them up in a dictionary when I need them.' Critically evaluate this statement and provide a better strategy using the feedback formula (something liked + something that didn't work + something to do differently next time).
guidedPractice.answer: Evaluation: While looking up words is useful, relying only on that prevents deep learning. Feedback: 'I liked that you are proactive about learning new words. What didn't work is that without using them, you likely won't remember them when you need them. Next time, after looking up a word, try to use it in a sentence or find it in another context to reinforce your memory.'

reteachModules.trigger: Student applies same reading strategies to informational texts as to fiction, ignoring text features and purpose.
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: Treating informational texts like fiction without adjusting reading stance.

miniLesson.explain: Informational texts provide information related to a particular idea, distinct from fiction. They use text features like organizers, graphic aids, and typographic effects to help locate and understand information. Unlike fiction, where you focus on plot and characters, reading informational texts requires you to extract information, evaluate evidence, and ask strategic questions: who is the author, what is their perspective, are there other justifiable conclusions?
miniLesson.example: Compare reading a short story (focus on feelings and plot) vs. a Grade 9 geography textbook (use index, headings, maps, and ask about the author's perspective on climate data).
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Switch gears: fiction → story; informational → facts & evidence.

guidedPractice.prompt: When reading a science article, what should you focus on instead of plot and characters?
guidedPractice.answer: Focus on extracting information, evaluating evidence, and using text features like headings and diagrams.

guidedPractice.prompt: Read the following excerpt from a New Forest National Park text: 'The park covers 219 square miles and includes ancient woodlands.' List two reading strategies you would use that are different from reading a novel.
guidedPractice.answer: 1. Use text organizers like the table of contents or headings to locate specific data. 2. Ask strategic questions: Who wrote this? What evidence supports the size claim? Is there another interpretation?

guidedPractice.prompt: Create a checklist of three adjustments you should make when switching from a fiction novel to an informational text. Explain why each is necessary.
guidedPractice.answer: 1. Preview text features (index, headings, graphs) – because informational texts are organized for quick reference. 2. Question the author's perspective and evidence – because informational texts present claims that may be biased. 3. Activate background knowledge – because connecting prior knowledge to new information deepens comprehension.

reteachModules.trigger: Student selects an option that ignores or undervalues background knowledge when reading informational texts.
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: Background knowledge is not important for understanding informational texts; the text itself should be sufficient.

miniLesson.explain: Background knowledge significantly impacts comprehension of informational texts. It helps you connect new information to what you already know, making it easier to understand and remember. Without activating prior knowledge, you may miss deeper meanings or struggle to evaluate the author's claims.
miniLesson.example: When reading a Grade 9 geography textbook, your knowledge of basic geography (like map reading and climate zones) helps you grasp new concepts. For the New Forest National Park text, recalling what you know about forests and parks allows you to better visualize and evaluate the information.
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Knowledge is the bridge: your background connects new ideas to old ones.

guidedPractice.prompt: True or False: Activating your background knowledge before reading an informational text can help you understand it better. Explain briefly.
guidedPractice.answer: True. Background knowledge provides a framework for new information, making comprehension easier and more meaningful.

guidedPractice.prompt: You are about to read a fire safety preparedness text. What background knowledge might you activate to help you read effectively?
guidedPractice.answer: You might recall what you know about fire hazards, safety procedures, or previous experiences with fire drills. This helps you connect the text's advice to real-life situations.

guidedPractice.prompt: A classmate says, 'I don't need to think about what I already know; the text gives me all the information.' Critique this statement using evidence about background knowledge.
guidedPractice.answer: This statement is wrong because background knowledge greatly impacts comprehension. The text does not stand alone; prior knowledge helps you evaluate evidence, draw inferences, and remember details. Without it, you may misunderstand or miss key points.

options: Immediately use a translation app to look up the word.
Try to guess the meaning from context clues first, then check a dictionary if needed.
Skip the word and continue reading.

questions.stem: Read this sentence from a history textbook: 'The treaty was a precursor to the war, setting the stage for conflict.' You do not know the word 'precursor'. Explain step by step how you would figure out its meaning without using a translation tool. Include at least one specific context clue from the sentence.
questions.rubric: Full credit (2 points): Student identifies context clue (e.g., 'setting the stage for conflict' implies precursor means something that comes before or leads to another event), makes a reasonable guess (e.g., 'something that happens before'), and states they would verify after reading. Partial credit (1 point): Mentions using context clues but does not identify a specific clue or process. No credit: Suggests using translation or gives irrelevant answer.

retestCards.passRule: All questions answered correctly. For open-ended, response must earn full credit according to rubric.

questions.stem: Two students are learning new vocabulary from an informational text. Student A spends 20 minutes memorizing the definitions and spelling of 8 new words. Student B spends 20 minutes writing a short paragraph using 5-6 of the same new words. Who is more likely to remember and correctly use the words next week?
options: Student A, because memorizing definitions builds a strong foundation.
Student B, because using words in context helps form lasting connections.
Both are equally effective if the same amount of time is spent.
Neither; vocabulary is best learned by only reading texts without writing.

questions.stem: Explain in 2-3 sentences why memorizing a list of vocabulary words without using them in sentences or contexts is an ineffective learning strategy. Include what the alternative should be.
questions.rubric: Student must state that memorization alone leads to quick forgetting because the brain lacks strong contextual connections. The alternative is to actively use new words in speaking, writing, or reading contexts to reinforce memory.

retestCards.passRule: Student must select the correct answer in Q1 (option 1) AND provide a response in Q2 that clearly explains the ineffectiveness of rote memorization without use and suggests active contextual use as an alternative.

Imagine the setting vividly.

dashboardFormat.objective: Informational texts provide information related to a particular idea, distinct from fiction.；Text features include text organizers (index, table of contents, glossary), graphic aids (maps, charts, diagrams), and typographic effects (bold, italics, font size).；Background knowledge significantly impacts comprehension of informational texts.

learningGoals.statement: Identify and describe the function of text features (organizers, graphic aids, typographic effects) in informational texts.
Adjust reading strategies based on text type (fiction vs. informational).
Apply background knowledge to enhance comprehension of informational texts.
Evaluate the effectiveness of vocabulary learning strategies, distinguishing between memorization and active use.
Critique over-reliance on translation tools for reading informational texts.

cards.question: When you see a table of contents and headings in a textbook, what is their main purpose?
options: To make the page look more interesting and break up the text.
To quickly locate sections and understand the organization of the content.
To add decoration between paragraphs.
To replace the need to read the full text.
cards.diagnosis: Check if student sees text features as functional rather than decorative.
misconceptions: Text features are not just decorative; they help readers navigate and understand the structure of the text.
✓ Correct! Table of contents and headings are functional tools that help readers find and organize information.
That is not their main purpose. They serve a navigational function.
They support reading, not replace it. You still need to read the text carefully.
cards.successCriteria: Recognizes that text features help locate and organize information.
cards.ossdExpectation: Reading for Meaning: read and demonstrate an understanding of a variety of informational texts.
cards.commonMisconception: Belief that features like headings and charts are only for decoration.

cards.question: A student always uses Google Translate for every unfamiliar word when reading an English informational text. Which statement best critiques this strategy?
options: It is efficient and helps you understand everything immediately.
It prevents you from practicing skills like inferring meaning from context and building inference skills.
It is the best way to learn new vocabulary because you see the translation immediately.
It is only bad if the translation is inaccurate; otherwise it is fine.
cards.diagnosis: Check if student understands the downside of heavy translation tool use.
misconceptions: While it may give quick answers, it prevents you from developing the ability to infer meaning from context.
✓ Correct! Relying on translation circumvents the active process of figuring out meaning, which is essential for language growth.
Seeing a translation does not necessarily lead to long-term retention or correct usage. Active engagement is more effective.
Even accurate translations can create dependency and reduce opportunities for deep processing of the language.
cards.successCriteria: Recognizes that over-reliance on translation hinders development of reading strategies like inferring meaning in context.
cards.ossdExpectation: Reading for Meaning: read and demonstrate an understanding of a variety of informational texts.
cards.commonMisconception: Belief that translation tools are always beneficial with no drawbacks for learning.

cards.question: A student memorizes a list of 20 new vocabulary words every week but never uses them in speaking or writing. What is the most likely outcome?
options: They will quickly forget most of the words because they are not used in context.
They will have a large, permanent vocabulary that they can use correctly.
Memorization is enough; they will be able to use the words correctly later.
They should only memorize words they see often; that would be more efficient.
cards.diagnosis: Check if student understands the ineffectiveness of rote memorization without active use.
misconceptions: ✓ Correct! Without active use, words fade from memory. Practice in reading and writing reinforces learning.
Memorization alone does not guarantee retention or correct usage. Context and use are essential.
Knowing a definition does not automatically translate to correct usage in sentences. Active practice is needed.
Frequency of exposure helps, but without use, even frequent words may not be retained or used well.
cards.successCriteria: Understands that memorization without use leads to poor retention and application.
cards.ossdExpectation: Reading for Meaning: read and demonstrate an understanding of a variety of informational texts.
cards.commonMisconception: Belief that memorizing definitions is sufficient for vocabulary learning.

cards.question: When reading a short story, you focus on plot and character emotions. When reading a science article, your reading approach should be:
options: The same, because all reading requires the same skills.
Focus on extracting information, evaluating evidence, and using text features like headings and diagrams.
Ignore text features and just read the paragraphs from start to finish.
Read faster to finish quickly, since it is just facts.
cards.diagnosis: Check if student understands that reading strategies need to be adjusted based on text type.
misconceptions: Different genres demand different approaches. Informational texts require you to extract information, evaluate evidence, and use text features.
✓ Correct! Science articles are informational texts; you need to read for main ideas, details, and to evaluate the author's claims.
Text features are designed to help you navigate and understand informational texts. Ignoring them makes reading less efficient.
Speed reading may cause you to miss important details and nuances. Informational texts require careful reading.
cards.successCriteria: Recognizes that different text types require different reading strategies.
cards.ossdExpectation: Reading for Meaning: read and demonstrate an understanding of a variety of informational texts.
cards.commonMisconception: Treating all texts the same way, ignoring text features and purposes.

cards.question: Before reading a passage about climate change, you recall what you already know about weather patterns. How does this help your reading?
options: It activates relevant schemas, making it easier to connect new information and understand the text better.
It is a waste of time because the text will provide all you need.
It only helps if you are an expert on the topic.
It might lead to bias, so you should avoid using it.
cards.diagnosis: Check if student values background knowledge as a reading strategy.
misconceptions: ✓ Correct! Prior knowledge provides a framework for understanding and evaluating new information.
Texts do not always provide all necessary background. Activating prior knowledge enhances comprehension.
Even partial prior knowledge can be helpful. It gives you a starting point for understanding.
Being aware of potential bias is good, but using prior knowledge is generally beneficial. You can also evaluate how the text confirms or challenges your ideas.
cards.successCriteria: Recognizes that prior knowledge facilitates comprehension and engagement with new information.
cards.ossdExpectation: Reading for Meaning: read and demonstrate an understanding of a variety of informational texts.
cards.commonMisconception: Underestimating or ignoring the role of background knowledge in comprehension.

cards.question: In an informational text, a map of the New Forest National Park is included. The best reason for this graphic aid is to:
options: To fill empty space on the page and make it look more professional.
Provide a visual representation of the area to help readers understand locations and spatial relationships.
To decorate the text and make it more colorful.
To replace the need to read the description of the park.
cards.diagnosis: Check if student understands that graphic aids are not decorative but convey specific information.
misconceptions: Maps serve a purpose: they provide visual information that supports the text.
✓ Correct! Maps, charts, and diagrams are functional tools that compress complex spatial data into an easily understood format.
While they may be visually appealing, their primary function is informational, not decorative.
Graphic aids complement the text; they do not replace reading. Both work together to convey information.
cards.successCriteria: Recognizes that graphic aids serve a functional purpose like providing spatial information.
cards.ossdExpectation: Reading for Meaning: read and demonstrate an understanding of a variety of informational texts.
cards.commonMisconception: Belief that charts and maps are only for decoration.

cards.question: When you look at the index of a textbook before reading, you are using a text organizer. This strategy is most helpful for:
options: Fiction novels, because they also have indexes.
Informational texts, because they often contain indexes to help you find specific topics quickly.
Poetry, because poems often have a glossary.
Any text equally; all texts have indexes.
cards.diagnosis: Check if student understands that text organizers are tailored for informational text navigation.
misconceptions: Indexes are rare in fiction; they are a feature of informational texts designed to help locate specific topics.
✓ Correct! Indexes are typical in textbooks and reference books, allowing you to scan for specific information before deep reading.
Poetry may have glossaries, but indexes are more associated with non-fiction. The question specifically asks about index.
Not all texts have indexes. They are most common in longer informational texts.
cards.successCriteria: Recognizes that text organizers like index are more common and useful in informational texts than fiction.
cards.ossdExpectation: Reading for Meaning: read and demonstrate an understanding of a variety of informational texts.
cards.commonMisconception: Treating informational texts like fiction without using their structural tools.

cards.question: Explain why memorizing vocabulary without using it in reading or writing is an ineffective strategy for learning English. Provide one specific suggestion for improvement.
cards.diagnosis: Check if student can critically evaluate a vocabulary learning strategy and propose improvement.
cards.successCriteria: Provides a clear reason and a concrete suggestion for active use.
cards.ossdExpectation: Reading for Meaning: read and demonstrate an understanding of a variety of informational texts.
cards.commonMisconception: Belief that memorization alone suffices for vocabulary acquisition.
